analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10 while making the E-Verify immigration check mandatory for all employers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on February 25, 2021 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10 an hour over three years — more slowly at businesses with fewer than 20 employees — and adjust it for inflation every two years. In exchange, it would make every employer in the country use E-Verify, a federal database that checks whether a new hire is legally authorized to work, within 18 months. It would also raise fines for hiring workers without authorization, let the government bar repeat violators from federal contracts, preempt state and local hiring laws, and cut off federal development grants to states that do not hand over driver's license records to the Department of Homeland Security. It died in committee without ever getting a hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the $7.25 federal minimum would get a raise phased to $10 over three years, with inflation adjustments after that. Employers would get a single uniform federal hiring-verification system, protection from stricter state laws, and a liability shield for good-faith reliance on the system. Companies selling identity-verification technology, and DHS, would gain a large new mandate and about $100 million a year in funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers and E-Verify technology vendors

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.00 immediately, then $8.75, $9.50, and $10.00 over three years, with businesses under 20 employees on a slower track reaching $9.25 at year three, and both minimums adjusted for inflation every two years.
Raises the youth minimum wage for workers under 20 from $4.25 toward $6.00 over three years and extends the time it can be paid from 90 to 180 days.
Permanently establishes E-Verify and requires all employers to use it on a phased timeline, with the largest employers complying within six months and everyone else within 18 months.

Raises civil penalties for hiring or referring unauthorized workers to $2,500-$25,000 depending on the violation, allows debarment of repeat violators from federal contracts and grants, and raises the criminal fine for pattern violators to up to $30,000 per unauthorized worker.
Preempts state and local laws relating to hiring or verification of unauthorized workers, giving employers one national standard.
Requires states to give DHS access to driver's license and identity card records for E-Verify, on pain of losing public works and community development block grants.
Transfers $100 million a year from the Treasury to DHS and authorizes another $100 million annually to run E-Verify.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear higher wage bills, with small firms getting the longest runway. Unauthorized workers would face losing their jobs when checks fail, and U.S. citizens and legal residents wrongfully flagged by the system could only sue the federal government under the Federal Tort Claims Act, with no class actions allowed. States refusing to share DMV data would lose federal development grants, and taxpayers would fund roughly $200 million a year for the verification system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, unauthorized workers, and flagged job applicants

drawbacks.text: Workers at businesses with fewer than 20 employees wait longer for every step of the raise — reaching only $9.25 after three years and $9.75 after four — and the bill keeps a separate, lower subminimum wage for new workers under 20 for up to 180 days.

The bill gives employers a broad good-faith defense: an employer that relies on E-Verify results cannot be sued or prosecuted for employment actions taken in good faith, and only 'clear and convincing evidence' of knowledge can defeat that defense.

A wrongfully flagged person's only compensation route is a claim against the federal government under the Federal Tort Claims Act, and class actions are barred — so database errors would fall on individual workers one at a time.

A national mandatory E-Verify check puts unauthorized workers at risk of job loss across the entire formal economy, and verification errors can also hit citizens and legal residents, while the bill pressures states to surrender driver's license records to DHS by withholding community development grants.
The $10 target is below the roughly $15 figure Democrats pursued the same year, so even supporters of a higher floor saw this as a smaller increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage increase is real but modest: $10 phased over three years, slower for workers at small firms, with a youth subminimum kept in place. The enforcement half of the bill is its heavier weight — a nationwide employment screening system that costs employers compliance effort, exposes unauthorized workers to job loss, gives flagged workers narrow legal remedies, and pressures states to share identity records. A supporter would call this a fair trade pairing wage growth with immigration enforcement; an honest one would have to acknowledge the wage number is low and the error-remedy provisions lean toward employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Cotton introduced the bill on February 25, 2021, joined by four Republican cosponsors: Senators Romney, Collins, Capito, and Portman.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's action history ends with the committee referral, and the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023.
The federal minimum wage remained $7.25 throughout the 117th Congress; the House-passed $15 increase stalled in the Senate, and this competing Republican version never advanced either.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, employers avoided both the wage increase and the nationwide E-Verify mandate, and the status quo held: the federal minimum wage stayed at $7.25 and E-Verify stayed voluntary for most employers. Low-wage workers, who would have gotten a raise, gained nothing. No single actor worked against the bill on the record — it simply was never scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill, though no roll-call exists because it never reached the floor.

industries.note: They would owe higher wages to minimum-wage staff, but businesses under 20 employees get up to a five-year phase-in, the bill preempts stricter state and local wage-and-hiring laws, and a good-faith defense shields them from lawsuits over hiring decisions. The raise is the workers' gain; the preemption and liability shield are the employers' gain.
Agricultural employers get an 18-month delay before the E-Verify mandate reaches farm labor, a carve-out that stretches the transition for an industry heavily dependent on unauthorized workers.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies, labor brokers, and union hiring halls
industries.note: The bill extends verification duties to recruiting and referring workers for pay, including hiring halls and labor-dispatch agencies, adding a compliance burden across the temp-staffing industry.

A universal E-Verify mandate plus roughly $100 million a year in federal funding creates a large government-paid market, and the bill explicitly counts use of secure identity-authentication technology in an employer's favor. The mandate's burden — submitting to screening — falls on every job applicant, not the vendor.
